title: Matching the Investment to the Timeline
tagline: The single rule that prevents most beginner disasters: the closer the goal, the safer the asset. Why retirement money and car-in-5-years money must never share a strategy.
summary: How time horizon determines asset choice, and the glide-path idea for protecting near-term goals.

sections.title: The core principle: time decides risk

paragraphs: Every dilemma like 'should I invest in FD or equity?' has the same answer: **it depends on when you need the money.** Equity has the highest long-term return but swings violently year to year. Given 15+ years, those swings average out and growth dominates. Given 2 years, a single bad year can leave you short exactly when the deadline arrives.
So you don't pick assets by what's 'best' in the abstract — you pick by **horizon**. Match the volatility of the asset to the time you have to recover from it.

blocks.title: Horizon → appropriate asset
rows: Hybrid funds, mix of index + debt
Equity index funds, ride the volatility

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Never put money you'll need within ~3 years into pure equity, and never leave money you won't touch for 15+ years sitting in FDs. The first risks a crash at the finish line; the second guarantees inflation eats your growth.

sections.title: Why short-term equity is so dangerous

paragraphs: Imagine Aarav puts his entire car down-payment into an equity fund with 18 months to go. The market drops 30% in month 16. He now has two bad choices: sell at a 30% loss and buy a smaller car, or delay the goal and hope for a recovery that may take years. Equity's volatility, harmless over decades, becomes a real threat near a fixed deadline.

The flip side is just as true: leaving a 30-year retirement corpus in FDs 'to be safe' is its own failure — a guaranteed loss to inflation over that span. Both mistakes come from ignoring the horizon.

blocks.title: Two pots, two strategies
blocks.text: This is why goals are kept separate. Aarav's emergency fund (always-available), his car fund (5-year, balanced), and any retirement SIP (30-year, equity) are three different pots with three different strategies — never one blended account where the wrong asset endangers the wrong goal.

sections.title: The glide path: de-risking near the finish

paragraphs: For a medium-term goal you can start with more growth and then **gradually shift to safety as the deadline nears** — a 'glide path'. Early on, when there's time to recover, you hold more equity for growth. In the final 1–2 years, you move the accumulated money into safe debt so a late-stage crash can't ruin a goal you've nearly funded.

items.title: Years 1–3: tilt to growth
items.detail: Hold a balanced mix (e.g. ~50–60% equity index, rest in debt) so the money compounds while there's time to absorb dips.

items.title: Year 4: start shifting
items.detail: Begin moving gains from equity into short-duration debt / RD, locking in growth as the deadline approaches.

items.title: Year 5: mostly safe
items.detail: Have the bulk in debt/FD so the final amount is predictable. You trade a little potential upside for certainty that the goal is funded.

blocks.text: The glide path captures most of equity's growth in the early years while removing the risk of a finish-line crash. It's the disciplined way to fund a goal like Aarav's 2031 car — which we'll build into a concrete plan in the next lesson.

cheatsheet: Pick assets by time horizon, not by what's 'best' in the abstract.
<3 years: capital protection (FD/RD, debt funds). >10 years: growth (equity index).
Never put money needed within ~3 years in pure equity; never leave 15+ year money in FDs.
Short-term equity risks a crash at the finish line; long-term FDs guarantee an inflation loss.
Keep each goal in its own pot with its own strategy (emergency / car / retirement).
Use a glide path: more equity early, shift to debt in the final 1–2 years to lock in the goal.

questions.prompt: Aarav has two goals: a car in 5 years and retirement in ~38 years. A friend says 'just put both in the same aggressive equity fund — equity wins long term.' Why is that wrong?
questions.hint: Do both goals have the same time to recover from a crash?
answer: Because the two goals have very different horizons, so they need different risk levels. The 38-year retirement money *should* be in aggressive equity — it has decades to ride out crashes. But the 5-year car money in pure equity is exposed to a finish-line crash: a 30% drop in year 4–5 could leave him unable to buy the car on time.
The fix is to separate the pots: equity for retirement, a balanced/glide-path mix for the car. Same person, same markets, but the timeline dictates a different strategy for each goal.
keyPoints: 5-yr money in pure equity risks a finish-line crash

questions.prompt: What is a 'glide path' and what problem does it solve for a medium-term goal?
questions.hint: How does the asset mix change as the deadline approaches?
answer: A glide path means gradually shifting a goal's money from growth assets (equity) toward safe assets (debt/FD) as the deadline nears. Early on you hold more equity to grow the corpus while there's time to recover from dips; in the final 1–2 years you move into safety so a late crash can't derail a nearly-funded goal.

It solves the core tension of medium-term goals: you want equity's growth *and* certainty at the finish. The glide path captures most of the growth early, then trades a little upside for protection right when you can least afford a loss.
keyPoints: Shift equity → debt as deadline nears
